7c2eb29e73294c4e1e9c2f9f34c95c44.text: A copper exploration company building a portfolio of high potential projects in B.C. and Western Australia has acquired a project adjacent to the Mount Polley mine northeast of Williams Lake near Likely. According to a news release Osiris Copper Corp. (Osiris One Metals Ltd.) entered into a binding Nov. 12 letter of intent to acquire the Miracle Gold Project that comprises two mineral claims covering approximately 6,300 hectares immediately west of Imperial Metals’ Mount Polley mine in the Quesnel Terrane. The Miracle Gold project is additionally located approximately 35 kilometres west of Canada’s second largest open pit copper mine, Trekor Metals’ Gibraltar Mine. It is covered by a B.C. exploration permit, valid to 2031, which authorises up to 50 surface drilling sites. “Miracle represents an attractive opportunity to advance a sizeable copper gold exploration property within one of British Columbia’s most established porphyry copper districts,” stated Osiris One Metals CEO Sreenath Didugu. “The project’s proximity to the Mount Polley and Gibraltar mines provides an important regional context. Particularly given the presence of mapped intrusive rocks, brecciation, alteration and historical copper anomalies across the property which have not yet been systematically followed up through a comprehensive modern exploration programme.” Osiris Copper Corp’s immediate focus according to Didugu will be on integrating the historical work with the exploration program completed this month to better understand the intrusive systems and refine priority targets. He said they believe the Miracle Gold Project has great geological potential, and its addition further strengthens Osiris’ portfolio of copper exploration assets in B.C. In June, Vancouver-based exploration company Inomin Mines Inc. announced the largest single exploration investment of $2.3 million at the Beaver-Lynx polymetallic project that is adjacent to the Gibraltar Mine.

05b11754c85a7e6ed37093e36415bc88.text: Doerkson orders SOGI materials out of B.C. schools | Williams Lake Tribune As one of his first orders of business, Premier Lorne Doerkson ordered materials and resources created through the Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity 123 schools initiative to be removed from government websites as he tries to wipe out a program he calls a “lightning rod for division.” “A lot of parents feel as though they haven’t had enough say in what their kids are being taught,” he said. “And I think that they have a point.” SOGI 123 is a set of resources introduced in B.C. schools starting in 2016 to prevent bullying. An organization called the ARC Foundation created and administered the resources but lost its contract with the government last summer, effectively ending SOGI as an active program. It is now up to individual school districts whether to continue using SOGI resources. B.C. Teachers’ Federation President Carole Gordon said this decision is “rooted in misinformation,” questioning what this will mean in practice and what specific resources will be removed. She also sought to reiterate that gender-diverse children need support in school. “Every child deserves to walk through the doors of their school feeling comfortable in who they are, knowing they have friends and adults in their corner,” Gordon said in a written statement. “We’ll always stand up for that.” Interim NDP Leader Jennifer Whiteside wants to know what those resources will be replaced with, noting SOGI’s success in reducing bullying. “That’s a serious question that both vulnerable youth and families and educators are going to want to understand,” she said. “What exactly is the plan?” B.C. 7f970d14a981cfe100c20958d95d2399.text: Police are keeping quiet about a chase through downtown Penticton. RCMP are keeping quiet about a recent video documenting part of a police chase through downtown Penticton. The video, posted to Instagram by Michelle Prystay, shows five police cruisers in pursuit of a white pickup truck along Nanaimo Avenue on Nov. 24. The pickup truck, with what appears to be a pair of ATVs strapped down in the bed, drives through the CIBC parking lot off Nanaimo Square, over the concrete parking stops and back into the street. As it drives over the concrete, the vehicle’s passenger falls out of the truck, and attempts to sprint down the road, stumbling into a faceplant in the middle of the intersection with Martin Street, before getting up and continuing to run down Nanaimo. The video does not show whether the individuals were taken into custody. The Penticton Western News reached out to the RCMP for comment, and the RCMP declined to share any information. “We are actively investigating this incident, and at this time are unable to provide any information to protect the integrity of our investigation,” said Const. Olivier Nielis, media relations officer with the RCMP. The video is titled GTA Penticton, referring to massively successful Grand Theft Auto video game franchise that saw its most recent release, GTA6, debut to millions of sales and high critical praise on Nov. 19.

165050294fe7515bb8273c7fa7fb437c.text: Doerkson orders B.C. public service to implement return -to-office plan | Williams Lake Tribune Doerkson orders B.C. public service to implement return -to-office plan Premier Lorne Doerkson is making moves to force public servants to return to the office. One of Premier Lorne Doerkson’s first acts since his cabinet was sworn in on Friday is to order Public Service head Kim Henderson to begin implementing a return-to-office plan for government workers. “The public servants who can work from the office will be back at it five days a week,” he said Wednesday (Nov. 25). Henderson is instructed to begin a phased return by reviewing existing remote work arrangements. Doerkson argues in-person collaboration will mean a more productive work environment. “This is about better service to British Columbians; people in the same room collaborate better, new employees get mentored by people who have been around, and ministries solve problems together,” he said. The premier also says this is a fairness issue, pointing out that many frontline government workers can’t work from home. “Nurses, doctors, teachers, correctional workers, and the people delivering frontline services show up in person every single day,” he said. “I think it’s reasonable to ask for people in our offices to do the same.” Doerkson says he’s been working in a near-empty office near the legislature, and still has no idea how many offices around the province are rented out but sit idle and under-utilized. B.C. General Employees’ Union President Paul Finch says he still has not met with the incoming government on this issue. He wants a better understanding of the government’s intentions and to get a chance to bring forward his members’ perspectives. That relief is in place until at least Dec. 31. GasBuddy doesn’t track the territories due to a lack of information there. De Haan said much of the drop is seasonal, with lower gasoline demand as the temperatures get colder. “Canadians and Americans alike, and broadly the northern hemisphere sees less gasoline demand. 4c67c2ef6dda2084233f52d65321dc63.text: Japanese national arrested in Ontario in connection with B.C. aggravated assault | Williams Lake Tribune Japanese national arrested in Ontario in connection with B.C. aggravated assault A Vancouver Police Department cruiser parked on Cordova Street on July 23, 2025. A suspect who was wanted on a Canada-wide warrant for aggravated assault in B.C. was arrested in Ontario recently. Yuki Saito, 20, was charged in October with aggravated assault stemming from an incident on April 25, 2025 when an unhoused man was allegedly assaulted and beaten in Stanley Park to the point of unconsciousness, according to a news release from Vancouver police Wednesday (Nov. 25). Saito was released on conditions following his arrest, but he failed to attend a scheduled court appearance. Police said that despite extensive efforts to locate Saito, investigators were unable to find him through “traditional investigative methods.” The suspect is a Japanese national on a student visa, Sgt. Adam Donaldson said. Investigator were given judicial authority to track a cellular device believed to be associated with Saito. On Friday (Nov. 20), investigators learned the suspect was in the York region of Ontario. Vancouver officers worked with York Regional Police, who located and arrested Saito without incident. Saito remains in custody and is expected to be returned to B.C.

174d5d24c0e101a56a31927150645fca.text: A 17-year-old was caught going almost 100 kilometres per hour over the speed limit in Maple Ridge over the weekend. The teen was stopped by the Maple Ridge RCMP Road Safety Target Team at around 9 p.m. Sunday evening going 175km/h in a 80km/h zone in the 27200 block of Lougheed Highway. A tier two excessive speeding ticket was handed to the driver for driving more than double the speed limit and police had their vehicle towed and impounded for seven days. “Needless to say, officers also had quite the conversation with this young person who will likely face a driving prohibition from the BC Superintendent of Motor Vehicles,” said Maple Ridge RCMP online. “Don’t let an open road be an invitation to test your vehicle’s speedometer. Slow down and drive safely, especially during this time of year with changing weather conditions,” RCMP added.

4d2688638cf81ef0ab5cf102693d83eb.text: The highest attendance for this year's Performances in Park at Boitanio Park in Williams Lake was on Aug. 6 with 312 people. It was another successful year of Performances in the Park despite attendance being down, according to the Central Cariboo Arts and Culture Society. At a Nov. 25 Central Cariboo Joint Committee meeting, executive director Melissa Normandin provided an overview of the free, family-friendly summer concert series that brought live music and cultural performances in Boitanio Park for Williams Lake residents and visitors from July 9 to Aug. 27. An average of 219 attendees were welcomed each evening, marking a small decrease from the 2025 season that had an average weekly attendance of 237. “Attendance was a bit down and I’m going to blame the weather for that,” Normandin said. Of the 16 different performers or acts participating in this year’s Performances in the Park seven were local. A total program budget of $36,155 supported through diversified funding sources including local government, community sponsorships and in-kind contributions. In June, Williams Lake First Nation was added as a core funding partner with the City of Williams Lake and Cariboo Regional District for a three year term that includes an annual payment of $22,000 to the society for eight summer events. Normandin said their budget dollars were pretty consistent with previous years, and if they had more they could probably review some different asks received from the community including shade and covered areas. Cleanliness and adequately supplied washroom facilities throughout the evening was another challenge, along with glass, and broken bottles and garbage. “We can tackle that, and hopefully work with the city on that,” Normandin said. Mayor Surinderpal Rathor said he attended every concert and encouraged organizers to keep up the good work. The highest attendance was on Aug. 6 featuring Sassafrass (Kimberly Kavanagh) along with Punjabi Gidha and Punjabi Bhangra performances

d7c5b3dcfa534ce8dd00b6c6534449b2.text: The Williams Lake Mustangs lose 4-3 against Merritt Centennials on Wednesday, Nov. 25 at Nicola Valley Arena, Merritt. The Williams Lake Mustangs stays atop in BCHC's Interior Division and second overall with 37 points. The Williams Lake Mustangs scored three straight goals in the second period to tie the game, but the Merritt Centennials scored the winner in the third to take the 4-3 victory on Wednesday, Nov. 25, at Nicola Valley Arena, Merritt. Merritt scored twice in the first period at 4:40 and 15:15 and added a third goal in the second period at 2:13 before Williams Lake answered at 3:57 with three straight in just under 11 minutes. Landon Gillanders got the Mustangs on the board with assists from Brenden Roberts and Dawson Knackstedt. Logan Hauk followed with an unassisted goal and Blake Collison tied it 3-3 at 14:55 with assists from Gillanders and Dawson Rowse. The Centennials regained the lead in the third period and held on for the win at 11:59. Mustangs goaltender Ivan Andersen stopped 37 of 41 shots. Merritt’s Nigel Alberts, Noah Lawless and Callum MacLean were named the game’s three stars. The loss came five days after Williams Lake beat Merritt 6-2 at home. The Mustangs also defeated the Columbia Valley Rockies 9-4 on Saturday, Nov. 21. Williams Lake remains first in the BCHC’s Interior Division and second overall with 37 points, three behind the Kimberley Dynamiters. The Mustangs visit the Princeton Posse on Saturday, Nov. 28 and the Summerland Jets on Sunday, Nov. 29. The Mustangs also play the Revelstoke Grizzlies on the road at the Revelstoke Forum on Friday, Dec. 4 at 7 p.m. They play there again Saturday, Dec. 5 at 7 p.m., then return home to host Merritt n Tuesday, Dec. 8.

The Downtown Williams Lake Winter Lights Festival: The World of Winter will take place on Saturday, Dec. 5 and include a 5 p.m. parade with a special visitor. Davis admittedly remembers starting as he believed he was going to make some money. “You don’t really make any but you can’t get more into the spirit of Christmas than doing this, and the people,” he said, smiling. “The people that come by and make comments, and that warms my heart.” Some of the many business windows Davis will be adding his touch to this holiday season in Williams Lake include Paradise Cinemas, Subway, Panago Pizza, Denny’s Restaurant and Sandtronic Business Systems Ltd. Adding a touch of joy when the sun drops and the night sky sets in are Christmas lights installed by staff with the City of Williams Lake. Director of Municipal Services Rob Warnock said light poles have been wrapped with a snowflake by the Tourism Discovery Centre and in front of Boitanio Mall. New this year are 22 wrapped poles up by Walmart at the Prosperity Ridge Shopping Centre. ”I love this time of year,” Warnock said. “I really get into doing the lights and I’ve noticed a lot of the guys have really gotten into it over the last several years now, so they’re pretty excited when we start putting stuff up.” Lights have additionally been installed throughout downtown Williams Lake, and Warnock said he hopes everyone enjoys them. Chats between the two reached upwards of 73,000 messages and were detailed in the initial charge. The filing also details conversations between the two that describe violence. 8fef20172b74b3f703ed253260e5564a.text: December is one of the riskiest times of the year for drivers across the Cariboo and B.C. With December less than a week away, Road Safety at Work put out a release reminding the public that a combination of snow, ice, low light and holidays makes driving particularly dangerous this time of year. An average of 37 crashes occur per hour in December, according to statistics provided by ICBC, while WorkSafeBC statistics indicate that December has the second-highest number of accepted motor vehicle incident time-loss claims. “December brings together several factors that can increase driving risk,” Trace Acres, spokesperson for Road Safety at Work’s Winter Driving Safety campaign, said. Between 2021 and 2025, 27,572 crashes were reported to ICBC during the month of December across B.C. In the North Central Region, which includes 100 Mile House, Prince Rupert, and Haida Gwaii and the rest of the north, there were 1,805 reported crashes. Road Safety at Work went on to note that snow and ice are not the only winter weather that impacts driving. Heavy rain can also reduce visibility and traction, while fog can make it difficult to judge distances. In addition, black ice can form even when the pavement appears clear. “As the days shorten, more morning and late afternoon trips are taking place in darkness. Drivers need to be especially alert for pedestrians, cyclists, roadside workers, and other road users,” Road Safety at Work said. In addition, holiday shopping, seasonal celebrations and family visits mean there are often more people travelling on unfamiliar roads this time of year. To help reduce crashes this December, Road Safety at Work recommends drivers postpone or cancel trips when possible. If this isn’t possible, there are several steps drivers can take. These include slowing down and leaving at least four seconds of following distance on highways and adjusting your speed according to weather conditions. It was taken to OWL to recover from head trauma that was apparently sustained during efforts to evade attacking crows. A barred owl found injured at The Beer Shack in White Rock was released in nearby Bakerview Park following a month of rehabilitation care at OWL in Delta. A barred owl rescued outside of a tavern in White Rock in mid-October has been released back into the wild following a month of rehab and recovery – but rest assured, its injuries had nothing to do with drinking and flying. OWL (Orphaned Wildlife Rehabilitation Society) bird manager Martina Versteeg said Tuesday (Nov. 24) that the call from The Beer Shack on Johnston Road was among at least three similar reports fielded that Oct. 12 morning regarding owls injured by window strikes/crow attacks. “It was a busy morning for OWL, I think it was already our third rescue before the centre opened for the day,” Versteeg said. “Two caring Good Samaritans helped out. One called it in while the other was able to wait for our volunteer, June.” June Young – who attended the scene with her husband, Gerry – said the owl “had been attacked by crows and was sitting on top of a newspaper or garbage can.” “He was very docile,” Young said. “(A second Good Samaritan) was leaning on the wall right beside him, and the owl easily let me take him with the net. “He did have head trauma, probably flew into a window whilst trying to escape the crows.” Versteeg said with the dark mornings and afternoons, “we are seeing more owls injured.” She encouraged people to be mindful when driving in the dark, as well as to make their home and/or business windows more visible by applying coverings. 73b0578faf1996e20e050da2bf3a68b4.text: The Prince George Humane Society has secured $2 million in commitments toward a $10 million animal welfare initiative for Northern B.C. Announced Nov. 23 in a press release by the Prince George Humane Society, the Community Welfare Initiative will focus on expanding access to veterinary care and developing modern sheltering and animal care facilities across the region. The society said the initiative will bring together two priorities: establishing a new Community Animal Hospital and improving sheltering and animal care facilities across the region. According to the release, the hospital will provide greater access to affordable veterinary services, preventive care, and spay and neuter programs. It will also operate a mobile unit that will travel to smaller and Indigenous communities throughout Northern B.C., bringing veterinary services to animals and families who have difficulty accessing care in Prince George. The project will be completed in phases, with the first focused on establishing the Community Animal Hospital and launching the mobile veterinary unit. According to the release, later phases will involve developing a modern sheltering and animal care facility to strengthen the society’s ability to rescue, rehabilitate and re-home vulnerable animals. The society said the initiative builds on 11 years of work supporting animals and the people who care for them in the community. “We believe that a community that can afford veterinary care is a community where fewer animals suffer, fewer pets are surrendered, and more families stay together,” Angela McLaren, CEO of Prince George Humane Society, said in the release.

99a780b2e05f0676484da3b1f559f2e3.text: Andrea Kathrein (fourth from left) and her daughter Makayla both received the Vital Link Award Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026, close to two years after they helped resuscitate their husband and father Blaine (third from left) after he suffered cardiac arrest. The Enderby man’s heart had stopped beating after he’d suffered a cardiac arrest Jan. 17, 2025 at his rural home. “Loving life, busy as ever, active,” he said Wednesday, Nov. 25. All because his wife and daughter refused to let him slip away. Andrea Kathrein spent 11 straight minutes performing rigorous CPR on her husband that January lunch hour. As responding paramedic Jeremy Vandekerkhove expressed, sustaining a successful CPR for that long isn’t easy. It’s physically demanding. You have to break ribs. “But honestly, when it’s your loved one, you do it,” he said. While Andrea was fighting for her husband’s life, daughter Makayla swiftly called 911. Their home is in rural Enderby so it took 11 minutes for the ambulance to arrive. When it did, Makayla directed the crew to her father, who was lying on the icy driveway where he’d collapsed. Things had seemed fairly normal just minutes earlier. Blaine had said he wasn’t feeling too good, and Makayla had given him an Aspirin. By some considerable stroke of luck, Andrea had come home for lunch that day, something she doesn’t usually do. A transportation manager for School District 83, Andrea has level one first aid training. Because Blaine was looking quite pale, they decided to go to the hospital. He collapsed on the way out to his truck to grab his wallet. When Andrea found him there, she hollered to Makayla. With 911 dispatch providing a good rhythm, Andrea put her CPR training to use in a real situation for the first time. “They just kept the counting really even,” she said of dispatch, “so I was able to just keep really focused (on doing chest compressions).” Andrea and Makayla served as the vital link between Blaine’s cardiac arrest and the arrival of paramedics,

NDP Leader David Eby called a snap election earlier in the day. A judge has approved adding Angelo Isidorou, principal secretary to new premier Lorne Doerkson, to a defamation suit launched last year by former Langley Township mayor Eric Woodward. An associate justice at B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver approved adding Isidorou, his company Fountainhead Communications, and Langley businessman John Cameron to the ongoing lawsuit. The Nov. 23 order noted that no lawyer appeared in court to represent Isidorou or Cameron. The lawsuit began in 2025 and has targeted numerous prominent Langley-area residents, including sitting Township Councillor Kim Richter and her husband Bob Richter, former longtime MLA and cabinet minister Rich Coleman, Langley businessman Thomas Martini, several companies, and a number of people involved in political communications. The suit was sparked by a string of anonymously posted videos and a blog post appearing on the Facebook pages Langley Township Watch and The Langley Monitor in late 2024 and early 2025. Woodward alleges he was defamed by claims in the video, which claimed that a “political insider” benefited from a special deal when the Township purchased new fire trucks. The lawsuit has targeted people who allegedly made or posted the videos and blog post. All of the current defendants have denied the claims against them, and none of the claims have been proven in a court of law. The lawsuit was initially launched against a dozen “John Doe” defendants, then over the spring of 2025 a series of court orders were used to discover the ownership of the websites and Facebook pages. Isidorou’s name came up in the case earlier, though he was not named as a defendant immediately. A high school student in Williams Lake is hoping to turn his passion for basketball into something that will benefit the community for years to come. Nathan Del Rosario has launched fundraising efforts to renovate the outdoor basketball court at Lake City Secondary School (LCSS) by May 2027. The push to collect $60,000 is part of Del Rosario’s capstone project. “I love basketball and I felt that the outdoor court needed a change,” he said. “If you’ve ever been to the court it has really deteriorated and is really slippery and even dangerous to play on.” Del Rosario said one of his friends was injured on the court with a torn ACL. This all set into motion the Grade 12 student, who is part of the senior basketball team and proudly represents Williams Lake at Basketball BC’s High Performance Academy Program in Langley, to pursue the idea of renovations to the LCSS basketball court as his capstone project. Mentoring Del Rosario is president of the Williams Lake Basketball Association (WLBA) Travis Nystoruk. “He’s a very ambitious individual,” Nystoruk said of Del Rosario. “And it’s such a great opportunity and a great project for not only capstone for graduation, but for the community and future of Williams Lake.” Nystoruk coached Del Rosario over the years through the WLBA and also school basketball teams. On Monday, Nov. 23, Del Rosario was joined by Nystoruk at Save-On-Foods where he held his first Pick a Square Fundraiser that pulled in $714. There are a total of 2,500 squares, equalling the area of the court, each available to purchase for a five dollar donation. Del Rosario said his main source of fundraising will be bottle donations, grants, sponsorships and public support. Supreme Court justice has acquitted a former Vancouver Island pastor of charges related to the alleged sexual abuse of youths who were receiving first aid treatment. Ryan Richard James Morgan, 43, formerly of Generations Church in Nanaimo, faced charges of sexual interference of a person under 16 years old and sexual assault for incidents that took place in Bella Bella, Nanaimo and Courtenay in 2017 and 2020. It involved two girls who were minors at the time and whose identities are protected under a publication ban. On Friday, Nov. 27, at the Nanaimo courthouse, Justice David Crerar said evidence presented during trial in totality, did not establish Morgan’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt nor that “any of the touches, as alleged, were made ‘for a sexual purpose’ or ‘in a sexual manner,’ as opposed to an accidental brush when checking and applying tape or ointment, [for] the purpose of treatment requested by a complainant.” Tania Holland, Crown counsel, had argued that Morgan, while at Generations Church, inappropriately touched the girls and in some instances, it involved applying K (kinesiology) tape, which was sometimes taped near the pubic area. During trial she described Morgan as “charismatic” and “well-spoken” who gained the trust of the accusers, who had vulnerabilities which she said Morgan exploited. He was in an authoritative position and used his clout to manipulate and exploit them. Owen James, defence counsel, called on witnesses that testified that Morgan was a “stickler” for following rules who ensured that leaders were not alone in a room with students, especially when it involved students of the opposite sex. As B.C.’s new Conservative government prepares to repeal Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity 123 (SOGI123) and strip the resource from schools, teachers in Vernon are pushing back, saying the anti-bullying resource is needed while questioning the rationale for its removal. Lisa LaBoucane, president of the Vernon Teachers’ Association (VTA), said Friday there are a lot of misunderstandings about SOGI, and suggested that Premier Lorne Doerkson and the Conservatives seized upon these misunderstandings to galvanize their base instead of correcting them in the lead-up to this fall’s provincial election. LaBoucane said it doesn’t appear that Doerkson himself has a strong grasp of what SOGI is, judging by his own comments. NDP MLA George Heyman is dead | Williams Lake Tribune George Heyman, B.C.'s former minister of environment and climate change strategy in Surrey on Friday, Dec. 15, 2023. The B.C. Prior to his time as a politician, the union said Heyman “joined the labour movement as a young logger and quickly became known for his commitment to union democracy, social justice, and organizing.” The union elected him as vice-president in 1987 and president in 1999. British Columbia’s First Nations leaders say they want to work with the incoming Conservative government, but have so far been sidelined amid signals of a more adversarial approach to Indigenous rights. “We need to meet with the premier, attorney general, and all the ministers, because I just want to get back to work,” said Robert Phillips of First Nations Summit and the First Nations Leadership Council in an interview. Premier Lorne Doerkson put Indigenous affairs front-and-centre in his mandate letter to new Attorney General Caroline Elliott, tasking her with repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act and defending private property rights against Aboriginal title claims. But First Nations leaders oppose any changes to or repeal of DRIPA, arguing it provides a reliable framework for government-to-government relations. They say repeal will create uncertainty, especially with so many large resource projects underway that rely on Indigenous consent. Phillips warns of “dire consequences” and endless court action if the DRIPA is repealed without something meaningful to replace it. Elliott is a well-known commentator on Aboriginal affairs, and holds a related PhD. But her stances stir controversy, especially her argument that Indigenous sovereignty can undermine democratic principles. She has called for not just the repeal of DRIPA, but constitutional change. “Just repealing one law isn’t enough,” she said in an Instagram reel released when she was running for Conservative leadership, adding, “I’ll lead the way on bold constitutional change because we can’t just sit by and accept the idea that it’s impossible.” In her first week as attorney general, Elliott declined interviews and held no press conferences. d8dc22d8947a0aa7ca0817fe2fc3599e.text: B.C. court dismisses suit challenging catholic hospital’s ban on MAiD procedures | Williams Lake Tribune B.C. court dismisses suit challenging catholic hospital’s ban on MAiD procedures The B.C. Supreme Court found that St. Paul''s Hospital can legally opt out of performing MAiD procedures. The B.C. Supreme Court has dismissed a Charter challenge seeking to invalidate a health ministry policy that allows religious hospitals to opt out of performing medical assistance in dying (MAiD) procedures. Chief Justice Ronald Skolrood found that when St. Paul’s Hospital transfers patients elsewhere to undergo MAiD, it does not violate a patient’s right to freedom of religion and life, liberty and security of the person or infringe upon a physician’s right to provide care in good conscience. St. Paul’s is a catholic hospital run by Providence Health Care, which prohibits its personnel from providing medical assistance in dying. The challenge was filed by the doctors and family of Sam O’Neill, a woman with stage 4 cervical cancer who elected to have MAiD while in treatment at St. Paul’s, but had to be transferred to a facility on the University of British Columbia campus for the procedure. Due to her pain level, she was sedated before being transferred, but never regained consciousness. The family argues the process caused O’Neill significant additional pain. Several other similar patient experiences were entered as evidence. O’Neill died in 2023. In 2025, the Vancouver Coastal Health authority opened a modular building near St Paul’s where patients can now receive MAiD without needing a vehicle transfer. While the judge writes that he does not wish to diminish or disregard the patients’ experience and pain, he does not find it to be a determining factor in whether Charter rights were violated. 6a681826a896258d340c6aa51ba293e1.text: Marion Craig performing sandbag lunges during a HYROX competition in Hamburg, Germany on Oct. 28, 2026. A Chilliwack woman has qualified to compete in a sporting world championship to be held in Hong Kong next year. Marion Craig, 65, placed first in her division and qualified for the Hong Kong championships during a Hyrox competition in Hamburg, Germany in October. Hyrox is a hybrid racing sport that combines running and exercises. The first event was run in Hamburg in 2017. A race consists of eight one-km runs, split up by exercises. Craig says that as a cross-country skier and CrossFit athlete and she was drawn to the sport because it involved performing exercises similar to what she was already doing while training, but were less technically challenging. “CrossFit has a lot of higher gymnastics, more complex technical moves that I just never really was very good at because I never did them as a kid,” Craig said. The eight exercises performed during a Hyrox race are: 1000 metres on a SkiErg, a machine which simulates the actions performed in cross-country skiing; a 50-m sled push; a 50-m sled pull; 80 m of burpee broad jumps; 1000 m on a rowing machine; a 200-m farmers carry; lunging 100 m while carrying a sandbag; and 100 “wall balls,” where the athlete squats facing a wall and tosses a ball to hit a target on the wall. Craig says she finds the wall ball portion to be the hardest as it takes place near the end of the race when “your heart rate’s already screaming.” “I find that one absolutely crippling,” Craig said. “That one is so hard for me, but it’s hard for a lot of people too.” Races are run in groups of 40. The first group begins the race and every 10 minutes another group begins. Racers can also choose to compete individually, in pairs or larger groups. Everyone in a group runs, but the exercises can be split in any way the group wants.
